stumbles.quote: On 2026-11-09, Oskar asked: "does that mean we could trim these to 256 length vectors without penalty by reversing the widening?"
stumbles.why: Oskar is unexplained, and "that" and "the widening" refer to an earlier conversation. The text never says what was widened or why.

stumbles.quote: Ettin-17m's final 256-to-768 output matrix folds into a 256-to-256 matrix.
stumbles.why: It doesn't say what is being folded or why this works. It also doesn't say how a 256-to-768 matrix can fold losslessly, for example because the 768 outputs lie in a 256-dimensional subspace.
"Remex" and "live index" are never defined. I can't tell what remex is (a quantizer?), where the live index runs, or what it is compared against.

stumbles.quote: Quantized search requires trading bit width against dimension count.
stumbles.why: This is stated as a requirement but not explained. The following numbers show a tradeoff, not a requirement.

stumbles.quote: Remex's rotation also folds into the 256-to-256 matrix so that the model emits rotated coordinates directly; with an int8 head, 4-bit codes reach 0.931 recall@10.
stumbles.why: The rotation, the "int8 head" and how it differs from the earlier 4-bit result (0.927) are all unexplained. It's unclear whether the head is quantized weights or something else.

stumbles.quote: The List Scout page runs the folded 256-dimensional model. Classifier answers are identical and fitting takes 1.2 s instead of 3.6 s.
stumbles.why: List Scout, the classifier and what is being fitted are never introduced, so the relevance of this paragraph is unclear.

stumbles.quote: Raising the bit width on 256 dimensions surpasses the live index at smaller sizes: 3 bits takes 104 bytes and reaches 0.868 recall@10
stumbles.why: The answer says quantized codes beat the live index in fewer bytes. The 8-bit code (264 bytes) is larger than the 200-byte live index, and 2-bit 256-dim is worse, so the claim holds only for some settings. Byte counts also aren't explained: 256 dims at 3 bits is 96 bytes, not 104.
hit@10 is not defined, and the text doesn't say how it differs from recall@10, which is measured against float search. The relevance labels and the 9,500 queries aren't described.

point: Ettin-17m embeddings can be cut to 256 dimensions with no loss in float search, and quantizing at 3–4 bits per dimension matches or beats the current 768-dimensional 2-bit index at smaller sizes, though the text relies on several undefined terms.
